title: The silver cup (Genesis 44)
hook: Judah, who once sold Joseph, offers himself in Benjamin's place

segments.voice: Yesterday, the brothers bowed in Egypt, admitted their guilt, and the governor turned away and wept. Which hidden tears did you notice? Day three hundred seventy-two.

The grain runs out. Jacob refuses, and refuses, to let Benjamin go. Finally Judah steps up: put him in my care, and if I don't bring him back, let me bear the blame forever. So the brothers return to Egypt with Benjamin. The governor throws them a feast, seats them in birth order, which unnerves them, and gives Benjamin five times as much as the others. They leave at dawn, sacks full, Simeon free, relieved. Then a man on the road behind them, hurrying. The governor's steward catches up: one of you has stolen my master's silver cup. They're so sure it's a mistake they say, whoever has it shall die. The steward searches, oldest to youngest. The last sack is Benjamin's.
screen: `JUDAH PLEDGES HIMSELF.` → `A FEAST IN BIRTH ORDER.` → `THE CUP IN BENJAMIN'S SACK.`

segments.voice: Joseph planted the cup. It's his last test. The brothers tear their clothes, and all of them go back with Benjamin. Then the governor offers them exactly what they once chose: the thief stays as my slave, the rest of you go home in peace. Here is the old situation set up again. A favored son of Rachel. A chance to be rid of him. And this time the brothers could even say it wasn't their fault. And Judah steps forward. This is the brother who said, years ago at the pit, let's sell him. Genesis has followed him since. In one chapter he wrongs his daughter-in-law Tamar, and ends up admitting she is more righteous than he is. Now he steps up to the governor and makes a long, careful plea. He tells the governor about their old father, who lost one son of the wife he loved, and whose life is bound up in the boy's life. If the boy doesn't come home, the old man will die. And then, in the King James Bible: "Now therefore, I pray thee, let thy servant abide instead of the lad a bondman to my lord; and let the lad go up with his brethren." "For how shall I go up to my father, and the lad be not with me?" Take me instead. The man who sold one brother into slavery offers himself as a slave to save the other. That is the change the test was looking for. Some Christian readers see in Judah a picture of the one who gives himself in another's place, and note that Matthew's Gospel traces Jesus's family line through Judah.
screen: `THE OFFER: KEEP THE THIEF, GO HOME.` · `JUDAH, WHO SAID SELL HIM.` · `JUDAH'S LONG PLEA.` · `TAKE ME INSTEAD OF THE LAD.` · then, large: `HOW SHALL I GO UP TO MY FATHER, AND THE LAD BE NOT WITH ME?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: offer yourself for someone else. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone near you who's carrying a load they can't really carry: a coworker, a sibling, a neighbor, a friend. Picture what it would look like to take some of it on: a shift, a chore, a hard conversation you could have so they don't have to. Not the whole thing. One piece. Notice what it would cost, and what it would give. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.
The silver cup. Joseph's cup, planted in Benjamin's sack as a final test, the test that showed Judah had changed.
Your line: take me instead. Today, quietly take one task off someone else's list, and don't mention it. Day three hundred seventy-two.

howItsDone: Some Christians read Judah's offer as a picture of substitution, someone giving himself in another's place, and preachers set it beside Jesus's death; Matthew 1 traces Jesus's line through Judah.

fork.reveal: "let thy servant abide instead of the lad a bondman to my lord." the brother who sold Joseph offers himself to save Benjamin.

original.note: Hebrew: Judah. Genesis links his name to praise, from his mother Leah's words at his birth.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a stolen cup.
what it means: a test that recreates the old crime, and a brother who once sold Joseph now offering himself instead.
what a scholar hears: the test rebuilds the scene at the pit, a favored son of Rachel and a chance to be rid of him, so Judah's plea (44:18–34) answers his own words in Genesis 37:26–27.

notes: 'The longest speech in Genesis' (Judah, 44:18–34) is a common commentary claim; softened in the voice and trapdoor to 'often called'. The on-screen card still reads THE LONGEST SPEECH IN GENESIS; confirm.
Benjamin's portion 'five times' as much (43:34); seating in birth order (43:33). Confirm.
Tamar episode (Genesis 38) summarized in one sentence; 'more righteous than I' (38:26) is paraphrased.
Etymology of 'Jew' from Judah (via Yehudi) is standard; confirm phrasing in the trapdoor.
Substitution typology offered as something Christians have often seen, not as the text's own claim.
